purpose: First deep-expansion pass: populate the standardized layer model with dense, evidence-aware records rather than empty schema fields.

identity.name: Roman Mithraic Mysteries
identity.social_profile: Predominantly male initiatory communities; membership is documented among soldiers, merchants, administrators and other urban/provincial populations.

formation.historical_field: Roman imperial religious pluralism, Iranian religious vocabulary, eastern Mediterranean cult practice and Roman association culture
formation.predecessor_questions: The relationship between Roman Mithras and Iranian Mithra remains debated; Roman Mithraism should not be treated as a simple unchanged continuation of Iranian worship.
formation.institutional_form: Small local communities meeting in mithraea rather than a centralized church.

worldview.cosmic_imagery: The tauroctony, sun imagery, celestial signs and planetary symbolism dominate surviving material evidence.
worldview.ritual_goal: Initiatory participation, communal belonging and engagement with a sacred cosmological drama; exact theological goals are partly unrecoverable.
worldview.afterlife: Astral interpretation is plausible in some scholarship, but the surviving evidence does not provide a complete standardized doctrine of salvation.

practice.initiation: Seven grades are attested in the fullest evidence: Corax, Nymphus, Miles, Leo, Perses, Heliodromus and Pater.
practice.ritual_roles: Grades carried distinctive symbols, clothing, ritual functions and planetary associations; the Pater occupied a leadership role.
practice.communal_meal: Mithraea commonly contain benches and dining arrangements associated with communal ritual meals.
practice.sacred_image: The tauroctony—Mithras killing the bull—is the dominant cult image, usually surrounded by astronomical symbolism.
practice.ladder_symbolism: A seven-step initiatory/cosmological ladder is reported in later interpretations, but specific ladder evidence varies by site and should not be universalized.

texts.primary_evidence: There is no surviving canonical Mithraic scripture.
texts.textual_limit: Most reconstruction comes from material evidence rather than internal doctrinal books.

people.named_figures: Individual priests and dedicators appear in inscriptions, but the movement lacks a securely documented single founder or prophet.
people.authority: Pater was the highest attested grade in the initiatory hierarchy.

organization.leadership: Local Pater figures are attested; no empire-wide central hierarchy is securely demonstrated.

geography.archaeology: Hundreds of mithraea and associated objects provide unusually rich material evidence for a religion whose internal texts are absent.

society.gender: Surviving evidence overwhelmingly associates participation with men; claims about universal exclusion should remain evidence-based by region and period.
society.military: Military personnel participated, but the cult was not simply a military religion; civilian dedicators are also documented.
society.empire: Its spread followed Roman imperial networks rather than a single missionary hierarchy.

relationships.related_to: Roman religious pluralism and Iranian Mithra vocabulary
relationships.historical_debate: The relationship to Christianity has been compared since antiquity, but resemblance does not by itself demonstrate direct borrowing.
relationships.modern_reception: Modern occult and popular culture frequently exaggerate or simplify Mithraic parallels.

evidence.confidence: high for existence, sites, grades and imagery; moderate-to-low for complete theology and ritual reconstruction
contested_claims: whether all members progressed through all seven grades
degree of continuity with Iranian Mithra worship

identity.name: Eleusinian Mysteries
identity.period: Bronze Age roots at Eleusis; historically documented institutional cult in Classical Greece through late antiquity

formation.historical_field: Greek polis religion, agrarian cult, mythic traditions concerning Demeter and Persephone and Athenian religious administration
formation.mythic_foundation: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter links the foundation of the rites to Demeter's search for Persephone and the establishment of sacred rites at Eleusis.
formation.institutionalization: The Athenian state became deeply involved in administration and protection of the mysteries.

worldview.central_problem: Human mortality and the uncertainty of death are central to the interpretive frame.
worldview.sacred_pattern: Loss, descent, return and renewal are expressed through the Demeter–Persephone myth.
worldview.initiation_goal: Initiation was associated by ancient testimony with blessedness or a more favorable condition after death, although the secret content cannot be reconstructed with certainty.

practice.preparation: Candidates underwent preliminary rites and purification before the major initiation.
practice.procession: Participants traveled from Athens toward Eleusis in a major sacred procession.
practice.fasting: Fasting formed part of the ritual sequence associated with Demeter.
practice.kykeon: The initiatory sequence included the ritual drink kykeon in the surviving tradition, though its exact role is debated.
practice.initiation: The Mysteries included Lesser Mysteries and Greater Mysteries, with stages of preparation and initiation.
practice.secrecy: Initiates were bound to secrecy; this is the principal reason the inner rite remains incompletely known.

texts.homeric_hymn: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter is a major literary source for the mythic foundation of the cult, but is not a transcript of the secret initiation.
texts.inscriptions: Epigraphic evidence documents administration, officials and participants.
texts.ancient_authors: Plutarch, Cicero, Pausanias and other ancient writers provide external testimony with differing purposes.

people.political_authority: Athens exercised substantial administrative authority over the sanctuary after incorporating Eleusis.

organization.sanctuary: The sanctuary at Eleusis was a large institutional complex centered on the Telesterion.
organization.membership: Initiation was open to a broad range of Greeks and, in some periods, others who met ritual requirements; linguistic and legal eligibility varied by period.
organization.hierarchy: Priestly families and civic authorities maintained ritual continuity.

geography.route: The Sacred Way connected Athens to Eleusis and formed the physical axis of the major procession.

society.politics: The mysteries demonstrate how a local cult could become integrated into the religious and political administration of a major Greek city-state.
society.gender: Women played major roles in the Demeter cult and initiation tradition, distinguishing it from many male-dominated associations.
society.social_range: Initiates crossed some ordinary social boundaries, though the sanctuary itself was administered through formal hierarchies.

relationships.mythic_parallel: Demeter/Persephone imagery became a major reference point in later discussions of death and renewal.
relationships.late_antiquity: The sanctuary survived for centuries before destruction in late antiquity.
relationships.modern_reception: Modern occult and psychological interpretations frequently reconstruct the secret rite beyond what the evidence securely permits.

evidence.confidence: high for sanctuary, procession, offices and initiation; deliberately low for the secret central revelation
unknowns: precise meaning of every sacred object

identity.name: Hermeticism
identity.period: Roman Egypt, especially 2nd–4th centuries CE; major Renaissance and modern revivals
identity.geographic_core: Egyptian Mediterranean intellectual centers, especially Alexandria and related environments

formation.historical_field: Hellenistic Egyptian religion, Platonism, Stoicism, Jewish and other late-antique intellectual traditions
formation.attributed_teacher: Hermes Trismegistus, a syncretic figure combining Greek Hermes and Egyptian Thoth
formation.development: Hermetic writings emerged as a corpus rather than as a single institution founded by a historical prophet.

worldview.ultimate_reality: Hermetic texts commonly describe a supreme divine reality, divine Mind, cosmic order and humanity's relationship to the divine.
worldview.anthropology: Human beings are presented as capable of knowledge of God and transformation through spiritual/intellectual awakening.
worldview.problem: Ignorance and forgetfulness separate human beings from divine knowledge.
worldview.goal: Gnosis—the transformative knowledge of God and the cosmos—is a recurring goal.
worldview.cosmology: Creation, Nous, Logos, celestial powers, material cosmos and ascent recur across the corpus, with significant variation between texts.

practice.contemplation: Meditative/intellectual contemplation is central in several treatises.
practice.prayer: Prayer and thanksgiving appear in the corpus.
practice.ascent: Some texts describe visionary or intellectual ascent through cosmic levels.
practice.magic_and_astrology: Later Hermetic traditions strongly intersected with astrology, alchemy and ritual magic; these should not automatically be projected backward onto every early Hermetic text.
practice.alchemy: Hermetic ideas became deeply intertwined with medieval and Renaissance alchemical literature.

texts.corpus_hermeticum: A collection of Greek philosophical-religious dialogues, transmitted as a collection in later manuscript tradition.
texts.asclepius: Latin Hermetic dialogue preserved independently and important for Western transmission.
texts.nag_hammadi: Hermetic writings also survive among the Nag Hammadi codices, demonstrating the wider circulation of Hermetic material in late antique Egypt.
texts.renaissance_transmission: Marsilio Ficino translated the Greek corpus into Latin in the 15th century, helping make Hermeticism a major Renaissance intellectual current.

organization.ancient_structure: No single church, centralized priesthood or continuous membership organization is securely demonstrated for all Hermetic literature.
organization.modern_structure: Modern Hermetic orders and magical societies created institutional structures influenced by Hermetic texts.

geography.renaissance_core: Florence and other European intellectual centers
geography.modern_core: Europe, North America and global occult networks

society.science: Hermeticism contributed to historical relationships among religion, natural philosophy, astrology and alchemy.
society.printing: Renaissance printing transformed Hermetic texts from elite manuscript circulation into a wider intellectual tradition.

evidence.confidence: high for the surviving textual corpus and its late-antique setting; lower for claims of a unified ancient Hermetic religion
contested_claims: degree of Egyptian versus Greek philosophical influence
whether Hermetic texts constituted a coherent organized religion

identity.name: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn

formation.field: Victorian occult revival, Freemasonry, Rosicrucianism, Christian esotericism and European ceremonial magic
formation.institutional_model: A graded initiatory society organized around temples and increasingly elaborate inner-order work.

worldview.goal: Structured occult study and ritual development leading toward adeptship.
worldview.cosmic_model: The Tree of Life served as an organizing map connecting divine names, planets, elements, Tarot, grades and ritual correspondences.

rituals: Lesser Banishing Ritual of the Pentagram
practice.advanced_work: Inner-order practice included construction and consecration of magical tools, visionary work and Enochian ritual systems.

texts.ritual_manuscripts: Cipher manuscripts and temple ritual papers formed a major body of internal instructional material.

people.major_conflicts: Disputes over authority, ritual control and Mathers/Crowley contributed to fragmentation and successor organizations.

organization.governance: The Three Chiefs were associated with Praemonstrator, Imperator and Cancellarius functions.
organization.membership: Progression depended on initiation, study and in some cases examinations.

geography.later_centers: Successor temples developed in Britain and elsewhere after fragmentation.

society.culture: Golden Dawn members contributed to literature, theatre, art and occult publishing.
society.gender: Women could hold significant positions in the order, notably Florence Farr and Moina Mathers, unusual relative to many contemporary male-dominated institutions.

evidence.confidence: high for organizational structure, grade system and surviving ritual manuscripts
contested_claims: ancient provenance of some order documents
exact chain of transmission for certain cipher materials

identity.name: Freemasonry
identity.period: modern institutional form from early 18th century; operative craft antecedents earlier
identity.geographic_core: Britain, then Europe and global expansion

formation.field: operative masonry, early modern fraternalism, sociability, Enlightenment culture and Christian-European moral discourse
formation.turning_point: Formation of the Grand Lodge of England in 1717 is a major institutional landmark for modern organized Freemasonry.
formation.constitution: The 1723 Constitutions became a foundational printed organizational text and spread rapidly internationally.

worldview.moral_framework: Self-improvement, fraternity, charity, duty, moral symbolism and personal discipline are central themes in mainstream Masonic self-description.
worldview.religion: Many jurisdictions historically require belief in a Supreme Being, while exact requirements vary by jurisdiction; Freemasonry should therefore not be treated as a single theology.
worldview.symbolic_cosmos: Architecture, geometry, light/darkness, building and Temple imagery form a major symbolic language.

practice.lodge: Members meet in lodges with officers, ritual openings/closings, degree ceremonies, lectures or symbolic instruction and social activity.
practice.charity: Charitable activity is an important public and institutional dimension.
practice.secrecy: Private ritual and recognition signs exist, but the existence and broad structure of Freemasonry are public.

texts.anderson_constitutions: The Constitutions of the Free-Masons, 1723, combined legendary history, charges, regulations and songs.
texts.ahiman_rezon: Antients Grand Lodge constitutional tradition, especially from 1756 onward.
texts.ritual_exposures: 18th- and 19th-century exposures provide external evidence for ritual development but must be distinguished from official constitutional documents.

people.later_figures: Freemasonry includes millions of members across many jurisdictions, with different constitutional histories.

organization.regional_unit: Provincial/District Grand Lodge in many jurisdictions
organization.governance: Jurisdictional rather than globally centralized; there is no single world Grand Lodge controlling all Freemasonry.

geography.documentary_marker: Benjamin Franklin printed an American edition of the Constitutions in Philadelphia in 1734.

society.enlightenment: The 1723 Constitutions articulated religious tolerance, merit, civility, education and self-improvement in an Enlightenment-era context.
society.politics: Lodges interacted with state, aristocratic, civic and intellectual networks, but conspiracy claims should be separated from documented institutional activity.
society.women: Mainstream regular jurisdictions historically excluded women, while women-only and mixed obediences later developed.

misconceptions: Templar-continuity claims are often legendary or jurisdiction-specific rather than demonstrated institutional continuity
Freemasonry is not synonymous with occultism

evidence.confidence: very high for modern institutional history and constitutional texts
contested_claims: exact relationship to medieval operative lodges
extent of political influence attributed to Freemasonry

identity.name: Thelema
identity.geographic_core: Cairo origin point; later Britain, continental Europe and North America

formation.field: Golden Dawn occultism, Victorian esotericism, Freemasonry, Rosicrucianism, yoga, ceremonial magic and Crowley's personal religious development
formation.birth_event: Crowley reported receiving Liber AL vel Legis in Cairo in April 1904 through the entity Aiwass.
formation.institutionalization: Thelema developed from a revelation into a broader religious-magical system through Crowley's writings and organizations.

worldview.central_law: Thelema interprets human existence through the discovery and fulfillment of True Will.
worldview.aeonic_model: Crowley organized Thelemic history around Aeons, especially the Aeon of Isis, Osiris and Horus.
worldview.goal: Self-realization, True Will, magical development and attainment within the Thelemic initiatory framework.

practice.magick: Thelemic Magick combines ceremonial ritual, meditation, invocation, visualization, symbolism and other practices.
practice.yoga: Crowley incorporated yogic and meditative disciplines into his broader system.
practice.ritual_calendar: The Gnostic Mass became an important communal ritual within O.T.O. and related bodies.
practice.initiation: Different Thelemic organizations use different degrees and initiation systems; they should not be collapsed into one hierarchy.

texts.central: Liber AL vel Legis / The Book of the Law
texts.commentary: Crowley produced extensive commentaries and instructional writings that became central to later Thelemic interpretation.

people.organizational_lineages: Different post-Crowley bodies disagree over succession and interpretation.

orders: various independent Thelemic orders and temples
organization.governance: No single uncontested institution governs all modern Thelemites.
organization.a_a: A∴A∴ presents a graded spiritual curriculum emphasizing individual attainment and instruction.
organization.oto: O.T.O. developed a fraternal/initiatory organizational structure with degrees and the Gnostic Mass.

historical_centers: Sicily through the Abbey of Thelema period
geography.modern: International networks exist in Europe, North America, South America and elsewhere.

society.counterculture: Thelema became associated with occult revival, counterculture, sexual politics and radical individualism, though its internal teachings are more complex than its popular image.
society.reputation: Crowley's notoriety substantially shaped public perception of the movement.
society.gender: Women such as Rose Crowley, Jane Wolfe and later female leaders played significant roles in its history.

influenced_by: Buddhist and Hindu practices as interpreted by Crowley
influenced: chaos magic and later occult subcultures in indirect ways

evidence.confidence: high for Crowley's writings, dates, organizations and textual corpus; lower for supernatural claims associated with Aiwass and magical effects
evidence.integrity: Record Aiwass as a reported religious revelation, not as independently verified supernatural fact.

identity.name: Modern Satanism: comparative cluster
identity.geographic_core: Initially Europe and North America; now global

formation.field: Christian Satan mythology, Romanticism, occultism, secularism, counterculture and modern identity politics
formation.classification: Modern Satanism is best modeled as a family of movements rather than a single doctrine.

worldview.laVeyan: The Church of Satan's Satan is principally a symbol of individualism, pride, carnality and opposition to conventional moral authority rather than a deity worshipped literally.
worldview.setian: Temple of Set theology treats Set as a metaphysical and initiatory figure and emphasizes Xeper/self-becoming.
worldview.satanic_temple: The Satanic Temple uses Satanic symbolism within a non-theistic framework emphasizing individual autonomy, compassion, reason and secular pluralism.
worldview.theistic: Some independent Satanists understand Satan as a real spiritual entity; these groups must be documented individually rather than inferred from the larger category.

practice.laVeyan: Ritual is often presented as psychodramatic or magical technology rather than worship of a literal Satan.
practice.setian: Setian practice emphasizes initiatory work, magical development and Xeper.
practice.activist: The Satanic Temple combines ritual/religious expression with public activism and legal challenges concerning religious liberty and church-state issues.

texts.setian: Setian corpus includes Aquino's writings and The Book of Coming Forth by Night.
texts.satanic_temple: Seven Fundamental Tenets and organizational publications.
texts.academic: Modern Satanism has a substantial scholarly literature in religious studies and sociology.

people.historical_context: Satanism also has a much older history as an accusation, literary symbol and theological category; that history must not be confused with modern self-identification.

organization.temple_of_set: Founded in 1975 following a major schism involving Michael Aquino.
organization.satanic_temple: Founded in 2013 and organized around non-theistic religious identity and activism.
organization.membership: Reliable global membership counts are unavailable; organizational self-reports should be distinguished from census data.

modern_centers: Australia and other countries through local groups and online networks
geography.media: Internet communication has become a major mechanism of contemporary Satanic community formation.

society.law: Satanic organizations frequently intersect with debates over religious freedom, public religious display, reproductive autonomy and church-state neutrality.
society.stigma: The category carries strong historical stigma because Christian polemics used Satanic accusations against religious opponents and marginalized groups.
society.moral_panic: 20th-century Satanic-panic narratives must be treated as a separate historical phenomenon from documented Satanic organizations.

relationships.historical_symbol: Satan derives from Jewish and Christian theological developments and later European literary culture.
relationships.occult: Modern Satanism intersects with Western esotericism but is not identical to occultism.
schisms: Church of Satan → Temple of Set, 1975

evidence.confidence: high for documented modern organizations and published texts; variable for independent groups and private practices
contested_claims: allegations based solely on hostile sources
